title: Isidasi's story
hookLine: three husbands sent her back; she tells the long tale behind it (Therigatha, Isidasi)

lines: TWO NUNS AFTER THE ALMS ROUND.
WHY DID YOU LEAVE THE WORLD?
cards: Two nuns sit together after the alms round, in the city of Pataliputta. One of them, Bodhi, asks the other a question that's half compliment and half puzzle. You're still young, and lovely, she says.
What did you see that made you leave the world? The other nun is Isidasi. She doesn't answer with a slogan.
She tells the whole story, and it's long, and it doesn't flatter anyone, not even herself.

teach.b: First, the faithful wife. Isidasi says she was married into a merchant family in Saketa, and did all a daughter-in-law was expected to do.
She bowed to her in-laws morning and evening, cooked, cleaned, served her husband with her own hands. And still he came to hate her. When his parents asked what she had done, she told them: nothing.
I've done no wrong. They sent her home to her father. Second, again and again.
Her father gave her to a second husband, who sent her back too. Then he invited a wandering beggar to stay as his son-in-law. Before long the man asked for his begging bowl and robe back, and left.

teach.h: TWICE MORE, AND NO FAULT FOUND.
teach.b: Three times, and no one could name a fault. So, with her father's blessing, she went forth. Third, the longer story.
Isidasi says she can now see her past lives: once a goldsmith who went after other men's wives, then long suffering, then births as animals, then hard human lives.

teach.h: BLAMELESS NOW, AND FREE AT LAST.
teach.b: In her telling, being sent away in this life was that old deed ripening. Fourth, how to hear it. Some readers find this ending hard, because it can sound like blaming a woman for being rejected.
But notice what the poem insists on first: in this life she did nothing wrong.
The past-life story is her searching out the whole shape of what happened, further back than one life, and then setting it down. She ends the poem free of all of it.

how: Isidasi's poem is read in Buddhist communities as a teaching on kamma across lives, and modern readers also discuss it as an account of a woman's marriages told in her own voice.

o: a wife's tale of the faults she confessed
a fable a monk told to warn young brides
a nun's whole tale of why she left home

p: asks why she left the world
where her first husband's family lived
asked for his bowl back and left
a past life, in her telling

s: Isidasi was sent away for being a bad wife
she says she served her in-laws and husband faithfully, and no one could name a fault.
the third man her father brought home was a wandering beggar
he stayed only a short while, then asked for his bowl and robe and left.
Isidasi answers Bodhi with a single line
she tells the whole story, from her marriages back through past lives.

games.q: you're Isidasi's father. your daughter has been sent back twice, and no one can say why. what do you do?
o: keep her at home and stop trying.
invite a wandering beggar to stay as her husband.
send her straight to the nuns.
games.why: he invites a beggar to be his son-in-law. before long the man asks for his bowl and robe and goes. only then does Isidasi go forth, with her father's blessing.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose life you know only by its headline: the divorce, the move, the illness, the job that ended.
Picture asking them, the way Bodhi asked Isidasi, how did it happen, and then not interrupting, not fixing, letting the story be as long as it is. Breathe into that patience.

wordCard.voice: Isidasi's story. Asked why she left the world, a nun told all of it: marriages that failed through no fault she could find, and a past that reached back through other lives. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali kamma (Sanskrit karma): deed, action. Isidasi traces this life's sorrow to a deed lives ago.

carryVoice: Your line: the whole story. Blameless in this life, and free at the end. See you tomorrow.
